claims.claim: Ignatius of Antioch was the third bishop of Antioch in Syria and died c. 108 as a martyr in Rome.
Ignatius wrote his letters while en route to Rome as a prisoner condemned to execution for his Christian beliefs during the reign of Emperor Trajan (98–117 A.D.).
From Smyrna, Ignatius wrote letters to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, and Rome; from Troas, he wrote to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and Polycarp the bishop of Smyrna.
The immediate purpose of most letters was to thank recipients for kindness shown to Ignatius, while the letter to the Romans aimed to prevent Christians there from saving him from martyrdom.
The seven epistles generally considered authentic are mentioned by the historian Eusebius in the first half of the fourth century.

Although the authenticity of his letters has been questioned, they continue to serve as an example of early Christian theology and address important topics including ecclesiology, the sacraments, and the role of bishops.
Modern critics are not unanimous about Eusebius's date of 108 A.D. for Ignatius's martyrdom, though there is general tendency to accept that he was martyred in Rome in the time of Trajan.

Ignatius's letters bear signs of being written in great haste, such as run-on sentences and an unsystematic succession of thought, and he modelled them after the biblical epistles of Paul, Peter, and John.
Ignatius is considered one of the three most important Apostolic Fathers, together with Clement of Rome and Polycarp.
